aspectTitle: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
aspectDescription: Links embedded in running text have their underline removed and are set in a color that differs from the surrounding body text by HUE only — there is no bold, italic, size, font-family change, and the link-vs-text lightness contrast is under 3:1. A sighted color-perceiving user can spot the links; a color-blind or grayscale user cannot tell them apart from prose. To flag this an evaluator must (a) recognize which colored spans are actually links (vs decorative emphasis) by reading the markup/meaning, (b) confirm hue is the ONLY differentiator, and (c) judge that any subtle non-color cue presen
scenario: Dark-mode coffee-industry editorial blog post. Four inline story links are brand blue #6f93cf with text-decoration:none and no weight/size/family/style change on near-white #e8e8ea body text over #0e0f12. Color-perceiving readers see blue; grayscale/color-blind readers cannot find the links.
mechanism: Link #6f93cf vs body #e8e8ea is 2.54:1 lightness contrast (under the 3:1 escape hatch), so hue is the sole differentiator; no underline, weight, italic, size, or hover/focus cue. Link-vs-bg 6.16:1 and body-vs-bg 15.66:1 both pass 1.4.3, which is why contrast scanners stay silent.

scenario: Sourdough-focaccia recipe blog using the literal F73 stylesheet pattern: a:link/a:visited/a:active have text-decoration:none (resting green #1f6f43), and only a:hover (plus a:active) add an underline and red color. No :focus rule, so keyboard users also get color-only at rest.

scenario: University LMS course page (HIST 214). The theme styles BOTH inline links (<a>) and lecturer emphasis (<strong>) with the identical maroon #9d1b3d + bold + no underline, so 'maroon+bold' is not a link-specific cue; half the maroon-bold phrases are reading-list links and half are non-link emphasis. scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (INAPPLICABLE / non-applicability boundary). Bank Acceptable Use Policy. Three inline clause hyperlinks (.inline-ref) are styled identical to neighboring static text: same color #202124, same weight, no underline, no hover/focus change. A normal blue underlined footer link is a distractor.
mechanism: Link color equals body color (1.00:1), so there is NO color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink and adjacent static text for anyone — full-color, color-blind, or grayscale. 1.4.1 protects information conveyed by color; here color conveys nothing about the link, so a color-blind user is at no disadvantage. aspectTitle: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
aspectDescription: A form marks required fields by coloring their labels (e.g. red) or adding a colored border, with NO asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, and no per-field text cue. The trap that demands human judgment: there may be a general instruction at the top, but it is itself color-keyed ('Required fields are shown in red') — which is useless to someone who cannot perceive red, since it never lets them identify WHICH specific fields are required. An evaluator must (1) see that color is the only visual distinction between required and optional labels, (2) confirm no per-field non-color cue exists, and (3)
scenario: Volunteer sign-up form (nonprofit/food bank). Required field labels are red (#c62828), optional labels black; that hue difference is the only required-vs-optional distinction. The sole instruction is the self-referential, colour-keyed 'Required fields appear in red' — which never lets a colour-blind user identify WHICH fields are required. No asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, no aria-required.
mechanism: Required fields identified by label colour (hue) only (F81); the 'alternative' instruction is itself colour-keyed and self-referential, so it provides no working visible non-colour means of identifying each required field as 1.4.1 demands.

aspectTitle: Error / validation feedback conveyed by color alone (red border or red text only) in the post-submit state
aspectDescription: After a failed submit (or during inline validation), fields that failed are outlined or tinted red, or have their label turned red, with NO error icon, NO inline error message, and NO '(error)' marker — the only signal that THIS field is wrong is its hue. Per F81 and Trusted Tester, an error indicator cannot use color alone. An evaluator must reach/observe the dynamic post-validation state, notice the erroring field is distinguished from valid fields purely by color, and confirm no adjacent non-color error cue exists. This is the 'prompting a response' limb (highlighting a field to prompt corr
scenario: Corporate timesheet login rendered in the post-submit error state: the failed password field gets a 2px red border while the still-valid email field keeps a 2px gray border. The red (#d92020) and gray (#8a8f94) borders are tuned to near-equal lightness so the grayscale 3:1 escape hatch does not apply. A generic banner ('We couldn't sign you in.') never names the password field; hue is the only per-field signal.
mechanism: F81 error-field-by-color-only: the only per-field cue that the PASSWORD is wrong is its red border hue, with no text/icon/marker; red↔gray luminance delta is below 3:1 so a color-blind/grayscale user cannot distinguish the invalid field from the valid one.

aspectTitle: Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact
aspectDescription: An informational bitmap or inline SVG (bar chart, line graph, status dashboard, map) uses color to encode a categorical fact, and it HAS a text alternative — but the alt/caption restates the data values and the color rule ('red bars indicate sales below quota') rather than RESOLVING it (naming WHICH employees fell below quota). Because the alt is present and plausible, an automated checker sees a satisfied alt attribute and passes; only a human who reads the alt against the picture sees that the color-borne distinction is never spelled out in text. This is the canonical F13 failure — 'alt exis
scenario: SaaS sales-analytics board-pack panel: a bar-chart (inline-SVG data: URI) of four reps' annual sales vs a $3.0M quota. Fred ($2.6M) and Bob ($2.2M) are drawn red (below quota), Mary/Andrew green. The alt lists all four figures and states 'the bars shown in red indicate sales below the yearly quota' but never names Fred and Bob. Canonical F13 case.
mechanism: F13 — alt restates the colour rule ('red = below quota') and all data values but omits the resolved fact (which reps are below quota); below-quota membership exists only as the red fill of the 2nd and 3rd bars in a raster image, reaching neither AT nor colour-blind sighted users.
primarySelector: figure img[alt^="Bar chart of FY24 annual sales"]

aspectTitle: Color-coded charts, maps, diagrams and game pieces distinguished by color with no pattern, icon, or in-graphic label (G111)
aspectDescription: Non-text graphics rely on solid color to distinguish categories — transit-map routes by color only, a bar/area chart whose series are told apart only by fill color matched to a color-only legend, a flow chart using green-background = pass / red-background = fail with no shape/label difference, an SVG diagram whose elements are identified by color with no number/legend pairing, or game pieces distinguished by color alone. Per G111 the fix is to ADD a pattern (hatching, dots, dashes), a distinct icon/shape, or an in-graphic text/number label so the same information survives without color. An eva
scenario: Inline-SVG transit/metro network map (Riverside Metro) with three routes (Crosstown/Harborline/Parkway) drawn as polylines that differ only by stroke color; every station on every line is an identical white dot, and the legend keys each route name to a solid colored swatch with no pattern, shape, icon, or in-line label.
mechanism: Route category is conveyed by line hue alone with no redundant non-color encoding; under CVD/grayscale the three strokes and color-only legend swatches collapse to near-identical greys and the identical dot stations give no fallback, so a sighted user who cannot distinguish color cannot follow a single route or match it to the legend (G111 'color + pattern/icon' not satisfied).

scenario: Retail-banking transaction list where credits are light-green and debits are dark-red text (large-bold).
